title: Fermilab SQMS Center Identifies Microscopic Origins of Qubit Performance Variance Across Superconducting Transmons - Quantum Computing Report
gist: A double-blind study of 22 superconducting transmons by Fermilab SQMS, Rigetti and partners links up to 2x T1 variance to nanoscale oxide thickness, trench depth and etch sidewall angle, while macroscopic defects do not matter. Rigetti is applying the findings to etching and passivation.

insights.claim: A multi-institution study led by Fermilab's SQMS Center with Rigetti Computing, NIST, Ames National Laboratory, Northwestern University and NPL, published in Applied Physics Reviews, isolates microscopic materials defects behind device-to-device performance variation in superconducting transmon qubits.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Signals that materials-level root-cause work, not just design, is now driving superconducting qubit yield.

insights.claim: Performance variance among identically designed qubits co-fabricated on the same substrate is described as a primary bottleneck to scaling fault-tolerant superconducting QPUs.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Yield uniformity, not just peak coherence, gates scaling; watch fabrication-process improvements.
insights.quote: A primary bottleneck in scaling fault-tolerant superconducting quantum processing units (QPUs) is performance variance among identically designed qubits

insights.claim: The study used a double-blind protocol on 22 transmon devices: teams cataloged features using seven spectroscopy and microscopy techniques without knowing coherence metrics, and coherence measured in the SQMS Quantum Garage was correlated afterward.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Blinded design increases credibility of the reported correlations, though 22 devices is a modest sample.

insights.claim: Single-nanometer shifts in surface oxide thickness, substrate trench depths below 20 nm and sidewall etch profiles together account for up to a twofold variation in T1 lifetimes across neighboring qubits on the same chip.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Tight nanometer-scale process control is a lever for coherence uniformity.

insights.claim: Sharp 10-15 degree etched sidewall angles, versus broad 30 degree tapered slopes, reduce electric field stored in lossy surface oxides and predict a 20%-30% T1 improvement.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Etch-profile engineering offers a concrete, quantified coherence gain.

insights.claim: Substrate trench depth variations below 20 nm drive sharp performance fluctuations, with effects saturating at deeper trench profiles.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Identifies a regime where process tolerance matters most.

insights.claim: Ambient surface oxide thickness dominates the dielectric loss tangent, and single-nanometer shifts directly drive up to a 2x variation in T1.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Surface passivation and oxide control are high-value process targets.

themes.theme: Macroscopic defects are not the culprit

insights.claim: Visible surface scratches, dust particulates and other macroscopic defects showed no statistical correlation with T1 variance; nanoscale interfaces dictate the coherence spread.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Inspection for visible defects is a poor yield proxy; metrology investment should target nanoscale interfaces.

insights.claim: Rigetti Computing is using these empirical parameters to optimize lithographic etching and surface passivation protocols, aiming for a predictive framework that enforces yield uniformity across multi-qubit processors.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Watch Rigetti for fidelity and yield improvements stemming from process changes.
insights.quote: providing a predictive framework to enforce yield uniformity across multi-qubit processors
